claim: shRNA-mediated knockdown of Rhou didn't affect the number of HF that are forming or their ability to grow in the dermis but revealed a PCP defect.
source: Finally, shRNA-mediated knockdown of Rhou expression didn't affect the number of HF that are forming or their ability to grow in the dermis but rather revealed what appeared to be a PCP defect, as reflected by the disorganization in the anterior:posterior directionality of the HFs (Figure 2I,J).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2I-J showing misoriented HFs upon Rhou knockdown.

claim: Three distinct Rhou shRNAs were enriched on average 3x relative to the 20 scrambled controls in the HF fraction of the screen triplicates.
source: We were particularly interested in RHOU, a Rho GTPase whose shRNAs were enriched on average 3x relative to the 20 scrambled controls in the HF fraction of our screen triplicates (Figure 3A). Moreover, in our screen, three distinct Rhou shRNAs exhibited this behavior, indicating a strong selective bias for downregulating this Rho during HF morphogenesis.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3A showing the enrichment of Rhou shRNAs.

claim: The enrichment of shRhou-transduced cells was not a consequence of enhanced proliferation of cells within the HF fraction.
source: Labeling of living embryos with 5-ethynyl-2'-deoxyuridine (EdU) to mark S-phase cells indicated that the enrichment of shRhou-transduced cells was not a consequence of enhanced proliferation of cells within the HF fraction (Figure 3B), further distinguishing this morphogenesis screen from our prior screens aimed at growth differentials.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3B showing no difference in EdU incorporation between shScr and shRhou cells.

claim: RHOU-deficiency did not significantly affect levels of the dozen other Rho GTPases, including closely related Rhov, which were expressed in skin epithelium at comparable or higher levels than Rhou.
source: We then performed RNA sequencing to show that RHOU-deficiency did not significantly affect levels of the dozen other Rho GTPases, including closely related Rhov, which were expressed in skin epithelium at comparable or higher levels than Rhou (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B showing RNA-seq data.

claim: Rhou mRNA expression was lower in placode than epidermal progenitors.
source: Rhou mRNA expression was lower in placode than epidermal progenitors (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, red box).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A showing transcriptome profiling data.

claim: RHOU protein localized cortically in embryonic basal epidermal progenitors, but its expression waned during HF morphogenesis.
source: Moreover, while RHOU protein localized cortically in embryonic basal epidermal progenitors, its expression waned during HF morphogenesis (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3E showing RHOU immunofluorescence at different developmental stages.

claim: RHOU's protein expression followed the same trend as its mRNA.
source: Pixel intensity quantification confirmed that RHOU's protein expression followed the same trend as its mRNA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C showing quantification of RHOU protein levels.

claim: Some Rhou-505 shRNA-transduced HFs were angled 180° relative to their normal orientation.
source: Most striking were some Rhou-505 shRNA-transduced HFs that were angled 1800 relative to their normal orientation (Figure 4A images and quantifications).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4A showing HF orientation analysis.

claim: Notable signs of defective PCP in RHOU-depleted skin included loss of asymmetric polarization of P-CADHERIN, NCAM and Sonic Hedgehog (SHH).
source: Other notable signs of defective PCP included loss of asymmetric polarization of P-CADHERIN, NCAM and Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), and an increase in follicles that grew straight downward (perpendicular to the skin surface) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A showing immunofluorescence of PCP markers.

claim: RHOU-depleted skin showed an increase in follicles that grew straight downward (perpendicular to the skin surface).
source: Other notable signs of defective PCP included loss of asymmetric polarization of P-CADHERIN, NCAM and Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), and an increase in follicles that grew straight downward (perpendicular to the skin surface) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4B showing quantification of perpendicular HFs.

claim: In WT embryos, embryonic epidermis exhibited a temporal increase of CELSR1 planar polarization along the anterior:posterior axis.
source: In WT embryos, embryonic epidermis exhibited a temporal increase of CELSR1 planar polarization along the anterior:posterior axis (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4C-D showing CELSR1 immunofluorescence and quantification over time.

claim: shRhou embryos showed clear perturbations in CELSR1 polarization.
source: In marked contrast, shRhou embryos showed clear perturbations in CELSR1 polarization.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4C-D showing CELSR1 immunofluorescence and quantification in shRhou embryos.

claim: The defects in CELSR1 polarization in shRhou embryos were not attributable to differences in the expression of core PCP genes.
source: These defects were not attributable to differences in the expression of core PCP genes, whose levels were comparable to controls (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4E showing RNA-seq data of PCP gene expression.

claim: shRhou basal epidermal progenitors were flatter than normal, with elongation of the basal surface where integrin-actin junctions reside, and reduced lateral surfaces, where adherens and PCP junctions interface with the actin cytoskeleton.
source: Closer inspection revealed that shRhou basal epidermal progenitors were flatter than normal, with elongation of the basal surface where integrin-actin junctions reside, and reduced lateral surfaces, where adherens and PCP junctions interface with the actin cytoskeleton (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3D showing immunofluorescence of shRhou skin sections.

claim: RHOU-depleted epidermis was thinner with reduced suprabasal keratin 10 (K10) and LORICRIN, and induction of keratin 6 (K6), a marker of aberrant epidermal behavior.
source: This resulted in a thinner epidermis with reduced suprabasal keratin 10 (K10) and LORICRIN, and induction of keratin 6 (K6), a marker of aberrant epidermal behavior (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-C showing immunofluorescence of differentiation markers.

claim: By E18.5, the barrier was largely intact in RHOU-depleted skin.
source: By E18.5, however, the barrier was largely intact (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D showing barrier assays.

claim: The epidermal sheet of E14.5 shRhou-transduced embryos showed considerably greater disorganization, with immature intercellular borders, as reflected by a broader distribution of P-CADHERIN.
source: By contrast, the epidermal sheet of E14.5 shRhou-transduced embryos showed considerably greater disorganization, with immature intercellular borders, as reflected by a broader distribution of P-CADHERIN and a failure to properly reorganize filamentous actin into a cortical network reflected by the increased in pixel intensity of F-ACTIN in the cytosol of shRhou-transduced cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5A showing whole-mount immunofluorescence and pixel intensity measurements.

claim: shRhou-transduced cells failed to properly reorganize filamentous actin into a cortical network reflected by the increased pixel intensity of F-ACTIN in the cytosol.
source: By contrast, the epidermal sheet of E14.5 shRhou-transduced embryos showed considerably greater disorganization, with immature intercellular borders, as reflected by a broader distribution of P-CADHERIN and a failure to properly reorganize filamentous actin into a cortical network reflected by the increased in pixel intensity of F-ACTIN in the cytosol of shRhou-transduced cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5A showing whole-mount immunofluorescence and pixel intensity measurements.

claim: Control basal epidermal cells were more cuboidal at E15.5 than earlier in development.
source: While control basal epidermal cells were more cuboidal at E15.5 than earlier in development (Z panels), basal cells from either shRhou-505 or shRhou-504 were flatter, a feature that accounted for their larger appearance in planar views, and substantiated our data from sagittal sections (Figure 5A Figure 5A; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and Figure 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5A showing Z-plane images.

claim: Basal cells from either shRhou-505 or shRhou-504 were flatter than control cells at E15.5.
source: While control basal epidermal cells were more cuboidal at E15.5 than earlier in development (Z panels), basal cells from either shRhou-505 or shRhou-504 were flatter, a feature that accounted for their larger appearance in planar views, and substantiated our data from sagittal sections (Figure 5A Figure 5A; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and Figure 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5A showing Z-plane images.

claim: The average area along the basement membrane of shRhou cells was larger than shScr counterparts.
source: Shape analysis of these cells within the E14.5 and E15.5 basal epidermal sheet revealed that indeed, the average area along the basement membrane of shRhou cells was larger than shScr counterparts, and this was accompanied by a marked decrease in their basal cell height, a feature still present at E16.5 (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5B showing quantification of cell area.

claim: shRhou cells showed a marked decrease in their basal cell height, a feature still present at E16.5.
source: Shape analysis of these cells within the E14.5 and E15.5 basal epidermal sheet revealed that indeed, the average area along the basement membrane of shRhou cells was larger than shScr counterparts, and this was accompanied by a marked decrease in their basal cell height, a feature still present at E16.5 (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5B showing quantification of cell height.

claim: Cell shape differences in shRhou cells resulted in a decrease in basal cell density.
source: Finally, these cell shape differences resulted in a decrease in basal cell density, which lessened concomitant with the natural increase in density that occurs during epidermal maturation (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5B showing quantification of cell density.

claim: The loss of RHOU was accompanied by an increase in the phosphorylation of myosin II light chain.
source: Consistent with this notion, the loss of RHOU was accompanied by an increase in the phosphorylation of myosin II light chain, expected from a more robust actomyosin network (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5C showing pMLC2 immunofluorescence.

claim: Upon shifting from low to high calcium medium to activate cell-cell junction assembly, RHOU-deficient epidermal cells exhibited clear delays in adherens junction formation.
source: Indeed, upon shifting from low to high calcium medium to activate cell-cell junction assembly, RHOU-deficient epidermal cells exhibited clear delays in adherens junction formation (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A showing E-CADHERIN immunofluorescence in calcium switch experiments.

claim: After 24 hr in high calcium, intercellular junctions in RHOU-deficient cells were indistinguishable from WT.
source: After 24 hr, however, intercellular junctions were indistinguishable from WT (not shown), indicating that RHOU-deficiency did not block intercellular junction formation per se.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the calcium switch experiments.

claim: RHOU appeared to function in supporting nascent adherens junctions at early stages of epithelial sheet formation, where adherens junction-linked actin dynamics are required.
source: Rather, RHOU appeared to function in supporting nascent adherens junctions at early stages of epithelial sheet formation, where adherens junction-linked actin dynamics are required (Vasioukhin et al., 2000).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the calcium switch experiments supported by a citation.

claim: Loss of RHOU resulted in an increase in F-ACTIN stress fibers and integrin-mediated focal adhesion size and length, features of reduced focal adhesion turnover.
source: Upon examining individual cells, it became clear that loss of RHOU resulted in an increase in F-ACTIN stress fibers and integrin-mediated focal adhesion size and length, features of reduced focal adhesion turnover (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B-D showing immunofluorescence and quantification of focal adhesions.

claim: Overexpression of RHOU resulted in PAK1/2 activation in keratinocytes.
source: Notably, overexpression of RHOU resulted in PAK1/2 activation in keratinocytes (Figure 6F) while depletion of RHOU resulted in its reduction (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6F showing immunoblots of pPAK1/2 levels upon RHOU overexpression.

claim: Depletion of RHOU resulted in reduction of PAK1/2 activation.
source: Notably, overexpression of RHOU resulted in PAK1/2 activation in keratinocytes (Figure 6F) while depletion of RHOU resulted in its reduction (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6G showing immunoblots of pPAK1/2 levels upon RHOU depletion.

claim: Activation of PAK1/2 inversely correlated with phospho-myosin light chain 2.
source: Moreover, we found that activation of PAK1/2 inversely correlated with phospho-myosin light chain 2, consistent with the view that RHOU functions by enhancing actin dynamics and focal adhesion turnover.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figures 6F-G showing immunoblots of pMLC2 levels.

claim: ARHGEF7 co-immunoprecipitates with MYC-RHOU in primary keratinocytes.
source: Among the uncharacterized proximity partners, we used immunoprecipitation and confirmed ARHGEF7's interaction with RHOU as well (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6H showing co-immunoprecipitation results.

claim: RHOU, ARHGEF7 and PAK2 co-localize in primary epidermal keratinocytes.
source: We further demonstrated the in vitro co-localization of these three proteins in primary epidermal keratinocytes (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6I showing immunofluorescence of the three proteins.

claim: The loss of PAK2 and ARHGEF7 yielded delays in adherens junction formation and cortical actin reorganization in the growing epidermal plane.
source: Turning to physiological relevance, we knocked down both Arhgef7 and Pak2 in skin epithelium in utero. Using a newly confirmed shArhgef7 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A) and a previously established Pak2 shRNA (Livshits et al., 2012), we found that the loss of these proteins yielded delays in adherens junction formation and cortical actin reorganization in the growing epidermal plane (Figure 6J and Figure 6—figure supplement 2B), without appreciably affecting the numbers of HFs that formed (Figure 6K).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6J showing whole-mount immunofluorescence of P-CADHERIN and F-ACTIN.

claim: Loss of PAK2 and ARHGEF7 did not appreciably affect the numbers of HFs that formed.
source: Turning to physiological relevance, we knocked down both Arhgef7 and Pak2 in skin epithelium in utero. Using a newly confirmed shArhgef7 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A) and a previously established Pak2 shRNA (Livshits et al., 2012), we found that the loss of these proteins yielded delays in adherens junction formation and cortical actin reorganization in the growing epidermal plane (Figure 6J and Figure 6—figure supplement 2B), without appreciably affecting the numbers of HFs that formed (Figure 6K).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6K showing quantification of HF numbers.

claim: PCP defects arose in the absence of PAK2 and ARHGEF7 and were manifested by the increase of HFs that grew straight downward.
source: Moreover, as we observed with RHOU loss, PCP defects arose in the absence of PAK2 and ARHGEF7 and were manifested by the increase of HFs that grew straight downward (Figure 6L).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6L showing P-CADHERIN immunofluorescence of hair pegs.

claim: While HFs were still specified in similar number upon sustained RHOU expression, their downward growth was markedly impaired in comparison to control or Rhou-depleted HFs.
source: While HFs were still specified in similar number upon sustained RHOU expression (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B), their downward growth was markedly impaired in comparison to control or Rhou-depleted HFs (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7B showing hair peg length quantification.

claim: Cells in RHOU-sustained buds exhibited a marked narrowing of their basal domain.
source: Probing deeper, the area occupied by individual placodes and total numbers of cells per placode remained largely unaffected, but cells exhibited a marked narrowing of their basal domain when RHOU was sustained (Figure 7C Z-plane images and Figure 7D).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7C-D showing placode shape analysis.

claim: While control columnar hair bud cells converted to a conical shape to achieve invagination, RHOU-sustained buds failed to reduce their apical cell surface and undergo this transition.
source: Thus, while control columnar hair bud cells converted to a conical shape to achieve invagination, RHOU-sustained buds failed to reduce their apical cell surface and undergo this transition.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7C-D showing placode shape analysis.

claim: Upon loss of RHOU, placode cells shifted to an exacerbated conical shape in comparison to wild-type placode cells, typified by a strikingly expanded basal cell domain, a reduction in apical F-actin and a corresponding shrinking of the apical area compared to control cells.
source: Conversely, upon loss of RHOU, placode cells shifted to an exacerbated conical shape in comparison to wild-type placode cells, typified by a strikingly expanded basal cell domain, a reduction in apical F-actin and a corresponding shrinking of the apical area compared to control cells (Figure 7E–G and Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7E-G showing placode shape analysis upon RHOU loss.

claim: The transition that HF placodes naturally undergo from a columnar to conical shape is driven by the downregulation of RHOU and associated changes in actin dynamics.
source: Taken together, our studies provided compelling evidence that the transition that HF placodes naturally undergo from a columnar to conical shape is driven by the downregulation of RHOU and associated changes in actin dynamics.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the gain and loss of function experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: Dampening of RHOU expression is essential for downgrowth of the follicle.
source: Moreover, our gain and loss of function experiments further demonstrate that this dampening of RHOU expression is essential for downgrowth of the follicle.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the gain and loss of function experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: By accentuating the conical cell shape required for HF invagination, shRhou cells acquire a competitive advantage for invasion and HF downgrowth over wild-type cells in a mosaic tissue.
source: Finally, these data imply that by accentuating the conical cell shape required for HF invagination, shRhou cells acquire a competitive advantage for invasion and HF downgrowth over wild-type cells in a mosaic tissue and are more likely to contribute to the HF (Figure 7H).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the screen results and functional data, illustrated in Figure 7H.

claim: 42% of the genes targeted by the library showed an enrichment or depletion of their targeting shRNA in either the epidermal or HF fractions.
source: That said, we were surprised to find that 42% of the genes targeted by our library showed an enrichment or depletion of their targeting shRNA in either the epidermal or HF fractions, revealing considerably less redundancy than previously assumed for Rho family members and their regulators.
evidence: This is stated as a result from the screen analysis.

claim: Both Rhob and Rac3 knockout mice are viable and fertile and don't show obvious defects during skin development.
source: In reflecting on the many hits we encountered, Rhob and Rac3 were surprising. Both Rhob (Liu et al., 2001) and Rac3 knockout mice (Corbetta et al., 2005) are viable and fertile and don't show obvious defects during skin development.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Some mechanisms of gene compensation that result from gene knockouts are not triggered upon RNAi-mediated knockdown.
source: An alternative explanation comes from recent studies by Didier Stainier's lab, which have show that some mechanisms of gene compensation that result from gene knockouts are not triggered upon RNAi-mediated knockdown (El-Brolosy et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: RHOU loss markedly perturbed the actin-driven formation of nascent adherens junctions, which arise during the narrow developmental window when planar polarization of CELSR1 takes place.
source: First, we discovered that RHOU loss markedly perturbed the actin-driven formation of nascent adherens junctions, which arise during the narrow developmental window when planar polarization of CELSR1 takes place.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the functional analyses shown in Figures 4-5.

claim: RHOU loss did not prevent the passive formation of adherens junctions that occurs in densely packed epithelial sheets.
source: Secondly, RHOU loss did not prevent the passive formation of adherens junctions that occurs in densely packed epithelial sheets.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the calcium switch experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: RHOU loss has not revealed intercellular adhesion defects in some contexts.
source: This explains why RHOU loss has not revealed intercellular adhesion defects in some contexts (Loebel et al., 2011), while in others, mislocalization of intercellular junction molecules has been described (Dickover et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of previous literature.

claim: In some contexts, mislocalization of intercellular junction molecules has been described upon RHOU loss.
source: This explains why RHOU loss has not revealed intercellular adhesion defects in some contexts (Loebel et al., 2011), while in others, mislocalization of intercellular junction molecules has been described (Dickover et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Initial links between PCP and Rho GTPases came from Drosophila, where parallels were found between PCP patterning phenotypes and hypomorphic RHOA mutations involving internal excisions in the protein.
source: Initial links between PCP and Rho GTPases came from Drosophila, where parallels were found between PCP patterning phenotypes and hypomorphic RHOA mutations involving internal excisions in the protein (Strutt et al., 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Dominant negative Rho mutations clearly disrupt PCP.
source: Although such dominant negative Rho mutations clearly disrupt PCP (Eaton et al., 1996), only triple/quadruple genetic mutants in Drosophila Rho GTPases have unveiled PCP phenotypes, and even those were mild (Muñoz-Descalzo et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Only triple/quadruple genetic mutants in Drosophila Rho GTPases have unveiled PCP phenotypes, and even those were mild.
source: Although such dominant negative Rho mutations clearly disrupt PCP (Eaton et al., 1996), only triple/quadruple genetic mutants in Drosophila Rho GTPases have unveiled PCP phenotypes, and even those were mild (Muñoz-Descalzo et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The worm RHOU orthologue, CHW-1, has been implicated as an upstream GTPase involved in vulval development.
source: Thus for instance, the worm RHOU orthologue, CHW-1, has also been implicated as an upstream GTPase involved in vulval development (Kidd et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Drawing a link between CHW-1 and PCP was only achieved with compound mutations involving other non-Rho pathway members.
source: That said, drawing a link to PCP was only achieved with compound mutations involving other non-Rho pathway members (Kidd et al., 2015), as were vertebrate studies on other Rho GTPases associated with regions of convergence-extension (Habas et al., 2001; Simões et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In the developing cochlea, a role for the two prototypical Rho GTPases RAC1 and CDC42 was shown to regulate auditory hair PCP.
source: In the developing cochlea, a role for the two prototypical Rho GTPases RAC1 and CDC42 was shown to regulate auditory hair PCP (Kirjavainen et al., 2015; Grimsley-Myers et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Mammalian RHOU is a key player in PCP establishment, and one that on its own, is sufficient to reveal strong PCP defects upon shRNA knockdown.
source: Our findings now place newfound emphasis on mammalian RHOU as a key player in PCP establishment, and one that on its own, is sufficient to reveal strong PCP defects upon shRNA knockdown.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the functional analyses shown in Figure 4.

claim: RHOU's function in governing PCP patterning in the skin is through the actin-mediated dynamics that drive adherens junction formation and dictate cell shape.
source: As our studies further reveal, RHOU's function in governing PCP patterning in the skin is through the actin-mediated dynamics that drive adherens junction formation and dictate cell shape.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the functional analyses shown in Figures 4-5.

claim: In a number of different cell lines in vitro, RHOU has been implicated as a regulator of focal adhesion dynamics, with elevated RHOU leading to focal adhesion dissolution and reduced RHOU favoring more stable focal adhesions.
source: In a number of different cell lines in vitro, RHOU has been implicated as a regulator of focal adhesion dynamics, with elevated RHOU leading to focal adhesion dissolution and reduced RHOU favoring more stable focal adhesions (Chuang et al., 2007; Ory et al., 2007; Ruusala and Aspenström, 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: p120-CATENIN is an established E-CADHERIN-binding protein which in polarized epithelia, exists in a complex with RhoGEFs/GAPs to alter associated Rho GTPases and affect apico-lateral junction stability.
source: While previously not identified as a RHOU-interacting partner, p120-CATENIN is an established E-CADHERIN-binding protein which in polarized epithelia, exists in a complex with RhoGEFs/GAPs to alter associated Rho GTPases and affect apico-lateral junction stability (Klompstra et al., 2015; Lang et al., 2014; Noren et al., 2000; Wildenberg et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In the foregut endoderm, RHOU is expressed in columnar and absent in more squamous tissues.
source: Further support this tantalizing notion comes from studies on the foregut endoderm, where RHOU is expressed in columnar and absent in more squamous tissues (Loebel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Rhou mRNA has recently been shown to be more highly expressed in the differentiated progeny versus the stem cells of the gut epithelium.
source: Intriguingly, Rhou mRNA has recently been shown to be more highly expressed in the differentiated progeny versus the stem cells of the gut epithelium (Slaymi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Inactivation of Rhou in gut increases significantly the level of pMLC2 and alters cell contractility.
source: Similarly to what we observed in the epidermis, inactivation of Rhou in gut increases significantly the level of pMLC2 and alters cell contractility.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison to the findings in the current study.

claim: In contrast to the developing epidermis, depletion of RHOU in the gut leads to an increase in cell proliferation and a reduction of apoptosis.
source: In contrast to the developing epidermis, however, depletion of RHOU in the gut leads to an increase in cell proliferation and a reduction of apoptosis, suggesting that RHOU signaling may be tailored to suit the particular needs of each tissue.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison to the findings in the current study, suggesting tissue-specific functions.

claim: Within the epidermal plane, assembly of a columnar epithelium, reinforced by RHOU-activated formation of a cortical actin band, favors adherens junction assembly and polarization of CELSR1.
source: Our studies revealed that within the epidermal plane, assembly of a columnar epithelium, reinforced by RHOU-activated formation of a cortical actin band, favors adherens junction assembly and polarization of CELSR1, which in turn will determine HF angling along the anterior-posterior axis (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a summary of the findings illustrated in Figure 8.

claim: Polarization of CELSR1 will determine HF angling along the anterior-posterior axis.
source: Our studies revealed that within the epidermal plane, assembly of a columnar epithelium, reinforced by RHOU-activated formation of a cortical actin band, favors adherens junction assembly and polarization of CELSR1, which in turn will determine HF angling along the anterior-posterior axis (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a summary of the findings illustrated in Figure 8.

claim: As HF morphogenesis proceeds, placode cells switch to a conical shape, displaying an accentuated basal and a constricted lateral-apical surface that facilitates invagination and hair bud downgrowth.
source: Emerging placode cells within the epidermal plane also begin by displaying an elongated shape. However, as HF morphogenesis proceeds, this cellular architecture soon wanes and the cells switch to a conical shape, displaying an accentuated basal and a constricted lateral-apical surface that facilitates invagination and hair bud downgrowth (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a summary of the findings illustrated in Figure 8.

claim: This process of hair bud invagination requires Myosin IIA, and Myh9 mutant hair buds often fail to invaginate.
source: This process requires Myosin IIA, and Myh9 mutant hair buds often fail to invaginate (Le et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: RHOU maintains epidermal architecture, but this antagonizes HF invagination and downgrowth.
source: Our findings now place RHOU at the crux of these actomyosin and cell shape dynamics that typify HF morphogenesis. As our gain of function studies revealed, RHOU maintains epidermal architecture, but this antagonizes HF invagination and downgrowth.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the gain of function experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: For HF morphogenesis to occur and for hair buds to invaginate, RHOU expression must be downregulated.
source: Thus for HF morphogenesis to occur and for hair buds to invaginate, RHOU expression must be downregulated.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the gain and loss of function experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: By accelerating the switch to a conical shape, downregulating RHOU stimulates the invagination process relative to RHOU-expressing cells.
source: Since Rhou shRNAs were selected for in the HF fraction of our screen, our findings further illustrate that by accelerating the switch to a conical shape, downregulating RHOU stimulates the invagination process relative to RHOU-expressing cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the screen results in light of the functional data.

claim: In early embryos derived from shRhou-transduced embryonic stem cells, the developing ventral foregut endoderm fails to maintain its apical position within the epithelium.
source: Our findings are interesting in light of prior studies showing that in early embryos derived from shRhou-transduced embryonic stem cells, the developing ventral foregut endoderm also fails to maintain its apical position within the epithelium (Loebel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: RHOU suppression may be a general feature of morphogenetic processes that require invagination from a RHOU+ epithelium.
source: Taken together, we speculate that RHOU suppression may be a general feature of morphogenetic processes that require invagination from a RHOU+ epithelium.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings in skin and previous studies in other tissues.

claim: PAK2 is the most highly expressed PAK1/2/3 protein in primary keratinocytes.
source: In primary keratinocytes and during epidermal development, PAK2 is the most highly expressed PAK1/2/3 protein and gene (Figure 6E, left and right respectively) that likely accounts for why PAK2 was more abundant than PAK1 in our proteomic analysis (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6E showing immunoblots and RNA-seq data.

claim: PAK2 is the most highly expressed PAK1/2/3 gene during epidermal development.
source: In primary keratinocytes and during epidermal development, PAK2 is the most highly expressed PAK1/2/3 protein and gene (Figure 6E, left and right respectively) that likely accounts for why PAK2 was more abundant than PAK1 in our proteomic analysis (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6E showing RNA-seq data.

claim: PAK proteins are known to bind RHOU.
source: PAK proteins are known to bind RHOU (Shutes et al., 2004), and RHOU can activate PAK1 (Tao et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: RHOU can activate PAK1.
source: PAK proteins are known to bind RHOU (Shutes et al., 2004), and RHOU can activate PAK1 (Tao et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: RHOU's interactome was enriched for proteins involved in 'adherens junctions'.
source: Gene ontology analysis (Figure 6D) revealed a RHOU interactome enriched for proteins involved in 'adherens junctions', including p120-catenin (Ctnnd1), a known RHOA-interacting protein (Perez-Moreno et al., 2006) and 'focal adhesions', including paxillin, integrin β1 and tensin-4, as well as NCK1, an adaptor protein required for Rho GTPase activation and cell migration (Saras et al., 2004), which was previously reported as an interactor of RHOU (Risse et al., 2013).
